verses.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and all his army, and all the kingdoms of the earth that were under his dominion, and all the peoples, were fighting against Jerusalem, and against all the cities of it, saying:

“Yahweh, the God of Israel, says, ‘Go, and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah, and tell him, Yahweh says, “Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it with fire.

You won’t escape out of his hand, but will surely be taken, and delivered into his hand. Your eyes will see the eyes of the king of Babylon, and he will speak with you mouth to mouth. You will go to Babylon.”’
“Yet hear Yahweh’s word, O Zedekiah king of Judah: Yahweh says concerning you, ‘You won’t die by the sword.

You will die in peace; and with the burnings of your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so they will make a burning for you. They shall lament you, saying, “Ah Lord!” for I have spoken the word,’ says Yahweh.”
Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah in Jerusalem,

when the king of Babylon’s army was fighting against Jerusalem, and against all the cities of Judah that were left, against Lachish and against Azekah; for these alone remained of the cities of Judah as fortified cities.
The word came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, after king Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people who were at Jerusalem, to proclaim liberty to them;
that every man should let his male servant, and every man his female servant, who is a Hebrew or a Hebrewess, go free; that no one should make bondservants of them, of a Jew his brother.

All the princes and all the people obeyed, who had entered into the covenant, that everyone should let his male servant, and everyone his female servant, go free, that no one should make bondservants of them any more; they obeyed, and let them go:
but afterwards they turned, and caused the servants and the handmaids, whom they had let go free, to return, and brought them into subjection for servants and for handmaids.
Therefore Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying,
“Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I made a covenant with your fathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, saying,

At the end of seven years, every man of you shall release his brother who is a Hebrew, who has been sold to you, and has served you six years. You shall let him go free from you; but your fathers didn’t listen to me, and didn’t incline their ear.
You had now turned, and had done that which is right in my eyes, in every man proclaiming liberty to his neighbor; and you had made a covenant before me in the house which is called by my name;

but you turned and profaned my name, and every man caused his servant, and every man his handmaid, whom you had let go free at their pleasure, to return; and you brought them into subjection, to be to you for servants and for handmaids.’”

Therefore Yahweh says: “You have not listened to me, to proclaim liberty, every man to his brother, and every man to his neighbor. Behold, I proclaim to you a liberty,” says Yahweh, “to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine. I will make you be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth.
I will give the men who have transgressed my covenant, who have not performed the words of the covenant which they made before me, when they cut the calf in two and passed between its parts:
the princes of Judah, the princes of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people of the land, who passed between the parts of the calf;
I will even give them into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their life. Their dead bodies will be food for the birds of the sky, and for the animals of the earth.

“I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his princes into the hands of their enemies, into the hands of those who seek their life, and into the hands of the king of Babylon’s army, who has gone away from you.

Behold, I will command,” says Yahweh, “and cause them to return to this city; and they shall fight against it, take it, and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.”

footnotes.content: The Lord's word comes to Jeremiah not in a quiet study but in the thick of siege—Babylon's armies encircle Jerusalem, and the city gasps. Even in the darkest moment, Yahweh speaks. This tells us something: His voice reaches us not when we've got everything in order, but when we're desperate and listening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The word comes with a hard truth: this city will fall to the king of Babylon, and fire will consume it. No soft words here. But notice—the Lord tells Zedekiah through His prophet. Even judgment comes wrapped in the offer to hear and respond. The king is being given a last chance to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is a terrible specificity here—Zedekiah will see the king of Babylon face to face, speak mouth to mouth, and be taken to Babylon. The prophecy strips away all escape routes. Yet even this word is meant to turn the king toward obedience, if only he will hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But listen—even in the shadow of captivity, there is a whisper of mercy. Zedekiah won't die by the sword. The Lord offers him a remnant of life, even if he loses his kingdom. Sometimes mercy looks like being spared the cruelest end, not spared all ends.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He will die in peace—not in battle, not in ignominy, but with the rites of his fathers. His people will lament him with 'Ah Lord!'—genuine sorrow. Even his grave will testify that he was remembered with honor. This small mercy, offered to a king who chose to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah speaks everything Yahweh has given him. In Jerusalem, under siege, with death pressing close, the prophet opens his mouth and delivers the word—comfort wrapped in judgment, warning wrapped in hope. Faithfulness doesn't depend on whether people listen; it depends on whether we speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lachish and Azekah stand as the last fortified cities—two garrison towns, all that's left of Judah's defenses. The geography of defeat narrows: the siege has done its work, and hope shrinks with every burned city. The prophet speaks in the grip of history unfolding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In desperation, Zedekiah and his people make a covenant to release their slaves—to proclaim liberty. Sometimes crisis brings clarity; pressed from without, the king turns inward and calls for justice. This covenant is good; it is right. But it will not last.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hebrew servants and handmaids go free. No brother is to be held in bondage by his brother. The law, remembered at last. You hear the echo of Exodus—the God who freed His people from Egypt now calls His people to free one another. Release is the shape of righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the princes, all the people who made the covenant, obeyed. They let the servants go free. For a moment, Jerusalem did what was right. Justice was done. The weak were lifted up. And the Lord saw it. But this is where the human heart shows its true scar.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then they turned. They brought back those they had freed and made them slaves again. The repentance was shallow, the obedience thin as frost. The moment the danger felt less urgent, the old sin crept back. This is the deepest betrayal—not that they failed, but that they had glimpsed righteousness and chose otherwise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The word comes again. Yahweh speaks into their apostasy. He will not look away from the turning back. The God who sees all acts—both the initial obedience and the fresh betrayal—opens His mouth in judgment. We cannot think He is too distant to notice our second sins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord recalls His ancient covenant with their fathers: the day He freed them from Egypt, from the house of bondage. That freedom was not earned or deserved; it was an act of pure grace. And He bound them to a law: remember your own freedom, and free one another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the end of seven years, Hebrew servants must go free. This was written into their law from the beginning—a rhythm that said: no one is yours to keep forever, only the Lord holds absolute claim. But their fathers didn't listen. The pattern of disobedience is very old.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet Zedekiah had done what was right—proclaiming liberty to neighbors, swearing the covenant before the Lord's house. The king's heart had turned. For that moment, they stood on the threshold of obedience. The Lord saw it. He marks every genuine turn toward righteousness, even when it doesn't hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then they turned and profaned His name by re-enslaving those they had freed. To profane the Lord's name is to take His character—His justice, His mercy—and spit on it by doing the opposite. They made themselves liars and thieves before the covenant they had sworn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Because they refused to proclaim true liberty to one another, Yahweh proclaims a different liberty—to sword, plague, and famine. The bitter irony: refusal to release one's brother invites the Lord to release His judgment. They will be 'tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth'—homeless, scattered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ancient ritual of covenant-making: they cut a calf in two and passed between its parts. The symbolism was stark—may I be like this if I break this oath. By breaking their covenant with the enslaved, they have stepped into the symbolic death they invoked upon themselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes of Judah, the princes of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people—everyone stood between those calf-parts and swore. The whole leadership, the whole city, bound themselves to justice. All of them will taste the judgment they drew upon themselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Into the hands of their enemies they will be given—those who seek to destroy them. Their dead bodies will feed the birds and beasts. It is a stark picture of abandonment and dishonor. This is what covenant-breaking costs: not just temporal loss, but the loss of dignity, the stripping away of honor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah himself, the king who began to do what was right, will fall into the hands of those who seek his life. Even the glimpse of righteousness could not save him from the judgment that comes upon those who turn back. He will face the king of Babylon not as a faithful servant but as a captive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord commands, and Babylon returns. Jerusalem will be besieged, taken, burned with fire. The cities of Judah become desolation. This is the end that was offered a chance to turn—and the city, through its rulers, chose the path that led here. Even judgment comes as the fruit of our own turning away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
